A.1.3 Formal definition CP(BI)RNNs

We begin by reviewing the basics of CP decomposition, before introducing a formal definition of CPRNNs, from which we also derive the definition of CPBIRNNs. More details on the single-layer versions of these models can be found in Lizaire et al. [2024].

First, recall that a CP decomposition of rank RR expresses a tensor 𝓣∈ℝd1×d2×d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}} as a sum of RR rank-one tensors: 𝓣=∑r=1R𝐚r∘𝐛r∘𝐜r≡[[𝐀,𝐁,𝐂]]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{a}_{r}\circ\mathbf{b}_{r}\circ\mathbf{c}_{r}\equiv[\![\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}]\!] where 𝐚r∈ℝd1\mathbf{a}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}, 𝐛r∈ℝd2\mathbf{b}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}} and 𝐜r∈ℝd3\mathbf{c}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}} (see, e.g., [Kolda and Bader, 2009]). The factor matrices 𝐀∈ℝd1×R,𝐁∈ℝd2×R,𝐂∈ℝd3×R\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times R},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times R},\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}\times R} have the vectors 𝐚r,𝐛r,𝐜r\mathbf{a}_{r},\mathbf{b}_{r},\mathbf{c}_{r} as columns. The CP decomposition reduces the parameter count from 𝒪⁡(d3)\mathcal{O}(d^{3}) to 𝒪⁡(R​d)\mathcal{O}(Rd) where d=m​a​x​{d1,d2,d3}d=max\{d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\}. We now turn to the definition of (multi-layer) CPRNNs.

Definition 4 (CPRNN).

A CP Recurrent Neural Network of depth LL, hidden size nn and rank RR is parameterized by initial hidden state vectors 𝐡0(l)∈ℝn\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, weight matrices 𝐀(l),𝐁(l),𝐂(l)∈ℝn×R\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\mathbf{C}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times R} (except for 𝐁(1)∈ℝd×R\mathbf{B}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times R}), 𝐔(l),𝐕(l)∈ℝn×n\mathbf{U}^{(l)},\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} (except for 𝐔(1)∈ℝd×n\mathbf{U}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}), bias terms 𝐛(l)∈ℝn\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and activation functions σ(l):ℝn→ℝn\sigma^{(l)}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} for l∈[L]l\in[L]. Given a sequence of inputs (𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱T)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},...,\mathbf{x}_{T}), a CPRNN outputs a sequence of hidden states (𝐡1(L),𝐡2(L),…,𝐡T(L))(\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(L)},\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)},...,\mathbf{h}_{T}^{(L)}) via the following computation at each time step t∈[T]t\in[T] and layer l∈[L]l\in[L]:

𝐡t(l)=σ(l)([[𝐀(l),𝐁(l),𝐂(l)]]×1𝐡t−1(l)×2𝐡t(l−1)+𝐕(l)𝐡t−1(l)+𝐔(l)𝐡t(l−1)+𝐛(l)).\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}=\sigma^{(l)}([\![\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\mathbf{C}^{(l)}]\!]\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}\times_{2}\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{t}+\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}+\mathbf{U}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{t}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}).

As in Definition 1 and 2, the activation functions σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} are applied element-wise. CPBIRNN is obtained from this definition by setting the first-order parameters (𝐕(l),𝐔(l),𝐛(l)\mathbf{V}^{(l)},\mathbf{U}^{(l)},\mathbf{b}^{(l)}) to zero. Moreover, note that the bilinear term of CP(BI)RNNs can be expressed using matrix product:

[[𝐀(l),𝐁(l),𝐂(l)]]×1𝐡t−1(l)×2𝐡t(l−1)=[𝐂(l)diag(𝐀(l)⊤𝐡t−1(l))𝐁(l)⊤]𝐡t(l−1).\displaystyle[\![\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\mathbf{C}^{(l)}]\!]\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}\times_{2}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l-1)}=\left[\mathbf{C}^{(l)}\mathrm{diag}({\mathbf{A}^{(l)}}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}){\mathbf{B}^{(l)}}^{\top}\right]\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l-1)}. (5)

A.2 Formalization of "linear RNNs compute linear transformations"

The following proposition formalizes the statement linear RNNs perform linear transformations of their inputs, regardless of the network’s depth.

Proposition 2.

Let h∈ℋRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L) be the function computed by a linear RNN. Then, for any TT, the function f:ℝd​T→ℝn​Tf:\mathbb{R}^{dT}\to\mathbb{R}^{nT} mapping (concatenations of) sequences of inputs (𝐱1,⋯,𝐱T)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{T}) to (concatenations of) sequences of hidden states (𝐡1(L),⋯,𝐡T(L))(\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{T}) is linear.

Proof.

We show that 𝐡t(L)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} for all t∈[T]t\in[T], which implies that their concatenation is in ℒd​T,n​T\mathcal{L}^{dT,nT}¶¶ ¶ Here (and thereafter), we use the abuse of notation 𝐡t(L)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} to mean that the function that maps (𝐱1,⋯,𝐱T)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{T}) to 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t} is linear.. The proof consists of a nested induction over ll and tt.

  • •

    Base case l=1l=1: We show that 𝐡t(1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{t}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} for all tt.

    • –

      Base case t=1t=1 : 𝐡1(1)=𝐔(1)​𝐱1+𝐕(1)​𝐡0(1)+𝐛(1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{1}=\mathbf{U}^{(1)}\mathbf{x}_{1}+\mathbf{V}^{(1)}\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{0}+\mathbf{b}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n}

    • –

      Inductive step on tt (proving for tt assuming true for t−1t-1): 𝐡t(1)=𝐔(1)​𝐱t+𝐕(1)​𝐡t−1(1)+𝐛(1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{t}=\mathbf{U}^{(1)}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\mathbf{V}^{(1)}\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} since by induction hypothesis 𝐡t−1(1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{t-1}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n}.

  • •

    Inductive step on ll: We show that 𝐡t(l)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{t}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} assuming 𝐡t(l−1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{t}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n}.

    • –

      Base case t=1t=1 : 𝐡1(l)=𝐔(l)​𝐡1(l−1)+𝐕(l)​𝐡0(l)+𝐛(l)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{1}=\mathbf{U}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{1}+\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{0}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} since 𝐡1(l−1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{1}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} by induction hypothesis.

    • –

      Inductive step on tt (proving for tt assuming true for t−1t-1): 𝐡t(l)=𝐔(l)​𝐡t(l−1)+𝐕(l)​𝐡t−1(l)+𝐛(l)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{t}=\mathbf{U}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{t}+\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} since 𝐡t(l−1)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{t}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} by induction hypothesis on ll and 𝐡t−1(l)∈ℒd​T,n\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{t-1}\in\mathcal{L}^{dT,n} by induction hypothesis on tt.

∎

A.3 Proof of Theorem 1

Theorem.

For any n>1n>1 and L≥1L\geq 1, ℋRNN​(n,L)⊊ℋRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1) for linear RNNs.

Proof.
Inclusion:

We first show that for any h∈ℋRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L), there exists a function h~∈ℋRNN​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h}, that is ℋRNN​(n,L)⊆ℋRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1). Consider the parameters of the RNN computing hh : {𝐔(l),𝐕(l),𝐛(l),𝐡0(l)}l=1L\{\mathbf{U}^{(l)},\mathbf{V}^{(l)},\mathbf{b}^{(l)},\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L}. First, we set the parameters of the first LL layers of the RNN computing h~\tilde{h} the same as the one computing hh so that the hidden states of the LthL^{\text{th}} layer are the same for both functions:

𝐔~(l)=𝐔(l),𝐕~(l)=𝐕(l),𝐛~(l)=𝐛(l),𝐡~0(l)=𝐡0(l)∀l∈[L]\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{U}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{V}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{b}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\quad\forall l\in[L]
⟹𝐡~t(l)=𝐡t(l)∀t​ and ​∀l∈[L].\implies\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(l)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}\quad\forall t\text{ and }\forall l\in[L].

Then, we set the last layer L+1L+1, such that it computes the identity over the hidden vectors of the previous layer 𝐡~t(L)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}:

𝐔~(L+1)=𝐈n,𝐕~(L+1)=𝟎,𝐛~(L+1)=𝟎,𝐡~0(L+1)=𝟎\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{I}_{n},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0}
⟹𝐡~t(L+1)=𝐈n​𝐡~t(L)+𝟎​𝐡~t−1(L+1)+𝟎=𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L).\implies\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{I}_{n}\;\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}+\mathbf{0}\;\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1}^{(L+1)}+\mathbf{0}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}.

This parameterization is such that 𝐡~t(L+1)=𝐡t(L)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} for all tt, which implies that h~=h\tilde{h}=h and proves the inclusion ℋRNN​(n,L)⊆ℋRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1). Note that this proof also works for nonlinear RNNs by applying the same principles: using the same nonlinearities for the first LL layers and leaving the last layer linear∥∥ ∥ Even in the case where the last layer has to be non-linear, one could find parameters such that the last layer approximates the identity operator to an arbitrary precision (assuming bounded domain of the inputs and infinite precision to represent floating operations)..

Strict inclusion:

To prove strict inclusion of this theorem, we consider the (real-valued) function fpf_{p} defined for any pp by

fp​(𝐱1,𝐱2,⋯,𝐱t)={(𝐱t−p)1 if ​t−p>00 otherwise.f_{p}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{t})=\begin{cases}(\mathbf{x}_{t-p})_{1}&\text{ if }t-p>0\\ 0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases} (3)

Informally, the function fpf_{p} copies the first component of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} pp time steps forward. To simplify the notation, let xt=(𝐱t)1x_{t}=(\mathbf{x}_{t})_{1} be the first component of the input at time tt. We first show in the following lemma that for any nn and any pp the function fpf_{p} can be computed by a linear RNN as soon as it is deep enough (at least p/(n−1)p/(n-1) layers).

Lemma 2.

For any n>1n>1 and p≥1p\geq 1, fp∈ℒn,1∘ℋRNN​(n,⌈p/(n−1)⌉)f_{p}\in\mathcal{L}^{n,1}\circ\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,\lceil p/(n-1)\rceil).

Proof.

The lemma is proved by construction. We consider an RNN computing a function hh and a linear mapping ww such that w∘h=fpw\circ h=f_{p}. In this RNN, each hidden vectors is the concatenation of the first dimension of nn consecutive inputs. At each time step, the input occupying the first units of the hidden vector jumps to the next layer while the others are sent to the next (in time) hidden state through the recurrent connection:

𝐡(1)t=[xt−(n−1)xt],𝐡(2)t=[xt−2​(n−1)xt−(n−1)],…,𝐡(L)t=[xt−L⁡(n−1)xt−(L−1)​(n−1)]\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{t}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{t-(n-1)}\\ \vdots\\ x_{t}\end{bmatrix},\quad\mathbf{h}^{(2)}_{t}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{t-2(n-1)}\\ \vdots\\ x_{t-(n-1)}\end{bmatrix},\quad\dots\;,\quad\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{t-L(n-1)}\\ \vdots\\ x_{t-(L-1)(n-1)}\end{bmatrix}

Since the depth of the network is L=⌈pn−1⌉L=\lceil\frac{p}{n-1}\rceil, the component 1+L⁡(n−1)−p1+L(n-1)-p of 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{t} contains xt−px_{t-p}. Moreover, it is ensured that, at all time, the first dimension of the previous pp inputs required for future computations are contained within the LL hidden vectors, see Figure 10.

This computation is achieved with the following weight matrices, null biases and null initial hidden vectors :

𝐔(1)=[001],𝐔(l)=††nicematrix-placeholder: bNiceArray (nicematrix)∀l∈[2,L] and 𝐕(l)=††nicematrix-placeholder: bNiceArray (nicematrix)∀l∈[L].\mathbf{U}^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\ \vdots\\ 0\\ 1\end{bmatrix},\quad\mathbf{U}^{(l)}=\begin{bNiceArray}\;\forall l\in[2,L]\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathbf{V}^{(l)}=\begin{bNiceArray}\;\forall l\in[L].

One can verify that by composing hh with the linear map w∈ℒn,1w\in\mathcal{L}^{n,1} defined by w⁡(𝐡)=[𝐡]1w(\mathbf{h})=[\mathbf{h}]_{1}, we obtain fpf_{p}, which verifies the statement of the lemma. ∎

We now show in the following lemma how the number of layers and hidden neurons needed for an RNN to compute the function fpf_{p} are lower bounded by the lag value pp.

Lemma 3.

If fp∈ℒn,1∘ℋRNN​(n,L)f_{p}\in\mathcal{L}^{n,1}\circ\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L), then p≤L⁡(n−1)p\leq L(n-1).

Proof.

In order to prove the lemma, we formalize the computation of fpf_{p} by an RNN as a flow graph in which information is propagated. The graph is a grid where the horizontal axis correspond to the time tt and the vertical axis to the depth ll. There is a total of L+2L+2 layers: one for the input (l=0l=0), one for the output (l=L+1l=L+1) and LL hidden layers in between. Each node can be identified by its layer ll and time step tt. Given the recurrent nature of the function, information can only flow through depth from ll to l+1l+1 or through the recurrent connection from tt to t+1t+1.

In order for an RNN to compute fpf_{p}, for each time step ii, the information of xix_{i} needs to flow through the graph up to 𝐡i+p(L)\mathbf{h}_{i+p}^{(L)} in the last layer pp time steps later. Thus, there exists a path in the graph between 𝐡i(1)\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(1)} and 𝐡i+p(L)\mathbf{h}_{i+p}^{(L)} through which the information of xix_{i} is propagated. Each step in this path is either horizontal or vertical, meaning either the information is propagated through recurrence, from 𝐡t(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} to 𝐡t+1(l)\mathbf{h}_{t+1}^{(l)}, or through depth, from 𝐡t(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} to 𝐡t(l+1)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l+1)}. See Figure 11 (center) for an illustration. Note that we will use both tt and ii to denote time steps, but we will use iis for information flowing through the network and tts for the actual time steps of the computation.

Now observe that for the information of xix_{i} to have been propagated through this path without loss of information, xix_{i} must have appeared as one of the components (neuron) of each of the hidden state appearing on this path**** ** One may argue that information about xix_{i} could have been separated between 2 or more neurons, but this would result in a sub-optimal construction since more than 2 neurons would have been used to store what could more efficiently be stored in a single neuron. . We now introduce a notation to formalize the flow of information through the computation network of the RNN.

Definition: For each i,t≥1i,t\geq 1 and 1≤l<L1\leq l<L, we let fi,t,l→=1f^{\to}_{i,t,l}=1 if the information of xix_{i} flows from tt to t+1t+1 at layer ll, and 00 otherwise; similarly, we let fi,t,l↑=1f^{\uparrow}_{i,t,l}=1 if the information of xix_{i} flows from ll to l+1l+1 at time tt, and 00 otherwise.

This definition is illustrated in Figure 11 (left). The computation fpf_{p} is schematized in the center part of the figure: the information of xix_{i} introduced at time t=it=i must flow out from the last layer of the RNN as the output at time t=i+pt=i+p.

Since it is introduced at time t=it=i, xix_{i} cannot flow out of the input at other times or flow horizontally from earlier times.

Lemma 3 is derived by inspecting the total information capacity needed across all layers at time tt, which is constrained by the number of neurons in the hidden states. At each time step tt, the sum of all information flowing in all the neurons in the hidden states cannot exceed the total size of the hidden states n​LnL (see the right panel in Figure 11). Formally, for all t≥1t\geq 1, we have

n​L≥∑l=1L∑i=1t−1fi,t−1,l→+∑l=1L∑i=1tfi,t,l−1↑.nL\geq\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}f_{i,t-1,l}^{\rightarrow}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}. (6)

The first part of the r.h.s. corresponds to the information that is flowing from the previous time step through recurrence (at the same layer), and the second one corresponds to the information flowing between two consecutive layers through depth (at time step tt).

The first double sum in Eq. (6) is simplified by observing that to compute fpf_{p}, all input information xix_{i} where i∈[t−p,t−1]i\in[t-p,t-1] must flow from t−1t-1 to tt. To achieve this, each input must flow horizontally in (at least) one of the layers, meaning that ∑l=1Lfi,t−1,l→≥1\sum_{l=1}^{L}f^{\to}_{i,t-1,l}\geq 1 for all i∈[t−p,t−1]i\in[t-p,t-1]. Hence, the first double sum can be lower bounded as ∑l=1L∑i=1t−1fi,t−1,l→≥p\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}f^{\to}_{i,t-1,l}\geq p, leading to

n​L≥p+∑l=1L∑i=1tfi,t,l−1↑nL\geq p+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow} (7)

for all time step t≥1t\geq 1. Since this inequality is true for any time step tt, we can sum up these inequalities for each time step up to an arbitrary time step KK to obtain

K​n​L≥K​p+∑t=1K∑l=1L∑i=1tfi,t,l−1↑, for any ​K.KnL\geq Kp+\sum_{t=1}^{K}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}\ ,\ \text{ for any }K. (8)

To lower bound the last term, first observe that to make its way from the input layer l=0l=0 to the last layer l=Ll=L, a given information xix_{i} must flow vertically at least once in each layer between the input and output times t∈[i,i+p]t\in[i,i+p]. Formally, we must have that, for each time step ii, ∑t=ii+pfi,t,l−1↑≥1\sum_{t=i}^{i+p}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}\geq 1 for all l∈[L]l\in[L], hence ∑l=1L∑t=ii+pfi,t,l−1↑≥L\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{t=i}^{i+p}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}\geq L. Again, since this inequality holds for each time step ii, we can sum up inequalities up to an arbitrary time step. In particular, we have

∑i=1K−p∑l=1L∑t=ii+pfi,t,l−1↑≥(K−p)​L, for any ​K≥p.\sum_{i=1}^{K-p}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{t=i}^{i+p}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}\geq(K-p)L\ ,\ \text{ for any }K\geq p.

Now, we can show that

∑t=1K∑l=1L∑i=1tfi,t,l−1↑≥∑i=1K−p∑l=1L∑t=ii+pfi,t,l−1↑.\sum_{t=1}^{K}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{K-p}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{t=i}^{i+p}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}.

Indeed, every term appearing in the r.h.s. is of the form fi~,i~+τ,l−1↑f_{\tilde{i},\tilde{i}+\tau,l-1}^{\uparrow} with i~∈[1,K−p]\tilde{i}\in[1,K-p] and τ∈[0,p]\tau\in[0,p], and thus appears in the l.h.s. as well when t=i~+τt=\tilde{i}+\tau (since in this case i~\tilde{i} is the range of the sum over ii of the l.h.s., which is [1,t]=[1,i~+τ][1,t]=[1,\tilde{i}+\tau]).

Finally, we thus have that ∑t=1K∑l=1L∑i=1tfi,t,l−1↑≥(K−p)​L\sum_{t=1}^{K}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{i=1}^{t}f_{i,t,l-1}^{\uparrow}\geq(K-p)L, which allows us to obtain from Eq. (8) the final inequality

K​n​L≥K​p+(K−p)​LKnL\geq Kp+(K-p)L

which can be re-arranged as

p≤L⁡(n−1)+p​LK.p\leq L(n-1)+\frac{pL}{K}.

Since this equality is true for any KK, we can choose KK large enough for p​LK\frac{pL}{K} to be strictly smaller than one, which implies the result, p≤L⁡(n−1)p\leq L(n-1).

∎

To prove the theorem, it only remains to combine the two lemmas. Let n>1n>1 and L≥1L\geq 1. We choose p=(L+1)​(n−1)p=(L+1)(n-1); from Lemma 2, fp∈ℒn,1∘ℋRNN​(n,L+1)f_{p}\in\mathcal{L}^{n,1}\circ\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1), from Lemma 3, fp∉ℒn,1∘ℋRNN​(n,L)f_{p}\not\in\mathcal{L}^{n,1}\circ\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L). This shows that ℋRNN​(n,L)⊊ℋRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1).

∎

A.4 Formalization of Proposition 1

Proposition.

For n>1n>1 and L>1L>1, a single-layer linear RNN of hidden size n​LnL has a greater latent representational capacity than a linear RNN of size nn and depth LL.

The following theorem formalizes the previous proposition.

Theorem 6.

Let ℋRNN(∥)(n,l)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,l) denote the set of functions h(∥)h^{(\|)} mapping an input sequence to the concatenation of hidden vectors computed at each layers of an RNN of hidden size nn and depth LL:

h(∥)(𝐱1,…,𝐱T)=(𝐡1(∥),…,𝐡T(∥)) with 𝐡t(∥)=[𝐡t(1)𝐡t(L)].h^{(\|)}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T})=(\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(\|)},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{T}^{(\|)})\quad\text{ with }\quad\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\|)}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\end{bmatrix}.

For any n>1n>1 and L≥1L\geq 1, ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)⊊ℋRNN(nL,1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1), for linear RNNs.

Proof.
Inclusion:

For any h(∥)∈ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)h^{(\|)}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L), we show there exists a h~∈ℋRNN​(n​L,1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1) such that h~=h(∥)\tilde{h}=h^{(\|)}, that is ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)⊆ℋRNN(nL,1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1). The idea is for the hidden vectors 𝐡~t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t} of the function h~\tilde{h} to be composed of LL blocks of nn dimensions. Each block reproduces the computation of one of the layer hidden vector 𝐡t(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} that is concatenated in the function h(∥)h^{(\|)}. The parameters of h~\tilde{h} are thus also separated in blocks as follow:

𝐡~t=𝐔~​𝐱t+𝐕~​𝐡~t−1+𝐛~→[𝐡~t,1𝐡~t,L]=[𝐔~1𝐔~L]​𝐱t+[𝐕~11…𝐕~1​L⋱𝐕~L​1…𝐕~L​L]​[𝐡~t−1,1𝐡~t−1,L]+[𝐛~1𝐛~L]\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{U}}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\tilde{\mathbf{V}}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1}+\tilde{\mathbf{b}}\to\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t,1}\\ \vdots\\ \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t,L}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1}\\ \vdots\\ \tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{L}\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{11}&\dots&\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{1L}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{L1}&\dots&\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{LL}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1,1}\\ \vdots\\ \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1,L}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{1}\\ \vdots\\ \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{L}\end{bmatrix} (9)

with 𝐡~t,l∈ℝn\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t,l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝐔l~∈ℝn×d\tilde{\mathbf{U}_{l}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, 𝐕~l​j∈ℝn×n\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{lj}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and 𝐛~l∈ℝn\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} for all l∈[L]l\in[L].

For each l∈[L]l\in[L], we want the computation 𝐡~t,l=𝐔~l​𝐱t+∑j=1L𝐕~l​j​𝐡~t−1,j+𝐛~l\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t,l}=\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{l}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\sum_{j=1}^{L}\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{lj}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1,j}+\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{l} to correspond to 𝐡t(l)=𝐔(l)​𝐡t(l−1)+𝐕(l)​𝐡t−1(l)+𝐛(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}=\mathbf{U}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}.

As shown in Corollary 2, 𝐡t(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} can be expressed in terms of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and 𝐡t−1(l¯)\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(\bar{l})} with l¯∈[l]\bar{l}\in[l] as :

𝐡t(l)=(∏i=1l𝐔(i))​𝐱t+∑j=1l(∏k=j+1l𝐔(k))​𝐕(j)​𝐡t−1(j)+∑j=1l(∏k=j+1l𝐔(k))​𝐛(j)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\mathbf{U}^{(i)}\right)\mathbf{x}_{t}+\sum_{j=1}^{l}\left(\prod_{k=j+1}^{l}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(j)}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(j)}+\sum_{j=1}^{l}\left(\prod_{k=j+1}^{l}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}\right)\mathbf{b}^{(j)}

It then suffices to set the parameters of an RNN computing h~\tilde{h} as

𝐔~l=∏i=1l𝐔(i),𝐕~l​j={(∏k=j+1l𝐔(k))​𝐕(j)j≤l0j>l,𝐛~l=∑j(∏k=j+1l𝐔(k))​𝐛(j)\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{l}=\prod^{l}_{i=1}\mathbf{U}^{(i)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{V}}_{lj}=\begin{cases}\left(\prod^{l}_{k=j+1}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(j)}&j\leq l\\ 0&j>l\end{cases},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_{l}=\sum_{j}\left(\prod^{l}_{k=j+1}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}\right)\mathbf{b}^{(j)}

in order to have 𝐡~t,l=𝐡t(l)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t,l}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} for all l∈[L]l\in[L], and therefore h~=h(∥)\tilde{h}=h^{(\|)}. This concludes the proof for ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)⊆ℋRNN(nL,1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1).

Strict inclusion:

We show there exists a function h~∈ℋRNN​(n​L,1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1) that cannot be computed by any function in h∈ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L), that is ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)⊅ℋRNN(nL,1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L)\not\supset\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1).

Consider the function h~∈ℋRNN​(n​L,1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1) computed by an RNN parameterized with 𝐕~=𝟎\tilde{\mathbf{V}}=\mathbf{0}, 𝐛~=𝟎\tilde{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{0} and 𝐔~\tilde{\mathbf{U}} block parameterized as in Eq. 9 with rank(𝐔~1)=1\rank(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1})=1 and rank(𝐔~l)=2\rank(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{l})=2 for all l∈[2,l]l\in[2,l]†††† †† In fact, the result works for any parameterization such that rank(𝐔~1)=1\rank(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1})=1 while rank(𝐔~l)>1\rank(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{l})>1 for at least one l∈[2,l]l\in[2,l]. Suppose there exists h∈ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h}. Then, we would have equality between the first hidden vectors 𝐡~1\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{1} and 𝐡1(∥)\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(\|)} which implies on one hand,

𝐡~1,1=𝐡1(1)\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{1,1}=\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(1)} ⟹𝐔~1​𝐱1=𝐔(1)​𝐱1⟹𝐔~1=𝐔(1)\displaystyle\implies\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1}\mathbf{x}_{1}=\mathbf{U}^{(1)}\mathbf{x}_{1}\implies\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1}=\mathbf{U}^{(1)}
⟹rank(𝐔(1))=rank(𝐔~1)=1,\displaystyle\implies\rank(\mathbf{U}^{(1)})=\rank(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{1})=1,

but on the other hand,

𝐡~1,2=𝐡1(2)\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{1,2}=\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(2)} ⟹𝐔~2​𝐱1=𝐔(2)​𝐔(1)​𝐱1⟹𝐔~2=𝐔(2)​𝐔(1)\displaystyle\implies\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{2}\mathbf{x}_{1}=\mathbf{U}^{(2)}\mathbf{U}^{(1)}\mathbf{x}_{1}\implies\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{2}=\mathbf{U}^{(2)}\mathbf{U}^{(1)}
⟹rank(𝐔(2)​𝐔(1))=rank(𝐔~2)=2\displaystyle\implies\rank(\mathbf{U}^{(2)}\mathbf{U}^{(1)})=\rank(\tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{2})=2
⟹rank(𝐔(1))≥2.\displaystyle\implies\rank(\mathbf{U}^{(1)})\geq 2.

The existence of h∈ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h} leads to a contradiction, proving that h∉ℋRNN​(n​L,1)h\not\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1) and ℋRNN(∥)(n,L)⊅ℋRNN(nL,1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}^{(\|)}(n,L)\not\supset\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(nL,1). ∎

A.5 Proof of Theorem 2

Theorem.

Considering linear RNNs with input dimension d=1d=1, let #​params​(n,L)\#\mathrm{params}(n,L) denote the number of parameters of a LL-layers RNN with hidden size nn ‡‡‡‡ ‡‡ One can check that #​params​(n,L)=(2​L−1)​n2+(L+1)​n\#\mathrm{params}(n,L)=(2L-1)n^{2}+(L+1)n (excluding initial hidden states as parameters count, though including them would not change the result)..

For any depth LL and for any hidden size n≥4n\geq 4, there exists a function f∈ℋRNN​(n,L)f\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L) such that, for all L~<L\tilde{L}<L and n~\tilde{n}, if f∈ℋRNN​(n~,L~)f\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\tilde{n},\tilde{L}) then #​params​(n~,L~)>#​params​(n,L)\#\mathrm{params}(\tilde{n},\tilde{L})>\#\mathrm{params}(n,L).

Proof.

Let L>1L>1 and n>1n>1. We set p=L⁡(n−1)p=L(n-1) and show that the function fpf_{p} defined in Eq. (3) satisfies the result. From Lemma 2, we know that fp∈ℒn,1∘ℋRNN​(n,L)f_{p}\in\mathcal{L}^{n,1}\circ\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L). Now, let L~\tilde{L} be an integer such that 1≤L~<L1\leq\tilde{L}<L and fp∈ℒn~,1∘ℋRNN​(n~,L~)f_{p}\in\mathcal{L}^{\tilde{n},1}\circ\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\tilde{n},\tilde{L}) for some integer n~\tilde{n}. Then, from Lemma 3, we must have p≤L~​(n~−1)p\leq\tilde{L}(\tilde{n}-1), i.e.,

L⁡(n−1)≤L~​(n~−1).L(n-1)\leq\tilde{L}(\tilde{n}-1).

It follows that

n~≥LL~​(n−1)+1.\tilde{n}\geq\frac{L}{\tilde{L}}(n-1)+1.

Since #​params​(n,L)=(2​L−1)​n2+(L+1)​n\#\mathrm{params}(n,L)=(2L-1)n^{2}+(L+1)n is monotonous increasing in nn for n≥1,L≥1n\geq 1,L\geq 1, a lower bound can be obtained as

#​params​(n~,L~)≥#​params​(LL~​(n−1)+1,L~)=(2​L~−1)​(LL~)2​n2+b​n+c\displaystyle\#\mathrm{params}(\tilde{n},\tilde{L})\geq\#\mathrm{params}\left(\frac{L}{\tilde{L}}(n-1)+1,\tilde{L}\right)=(2\tilde{L}-1)\left(\frac{L}{\tilde{L}}\right)^{2}n^{2}+bn+c

where bb and cc are constants that depend only on LL and L~\tilde{L}. It follows that

#​params​(n~,L~)−#​params​(n,L)≥((2​L~−1)​(LL~)2−2​L+1)​n2+b′​n+c\#\mathrm{params}(\tilde{n},\tilde{L})-\#\mathrm{params}(n,L)\geq\left((2\tilde{L}-1)\left(\frac{L}{\tilde{L}}\right)^{2}-2L+1\right)n^{2}+b^{\prime}n+c (10)

where b′b^{\prime} does not depend on nn.

The r.h.s. of Eq. (10) is a second order polynomial in nn and its leading coefficient is positive. To see this, this coefficient can be developped and re-arranged as

a=(L−L~)​(2​L~​L−L−L~)L~2>0.a=\frac{(L-\tilde{L})(2\tilde{L}L-L-\tilde{L})}{\tilde{L}^{2}}>0. (11)

All factors L~−2\tilde{L}^{-2}, L−L~L-\tilde{L} and 2​L~​L−(L~+L)2\tilde{L}L-(\tilde{L}+L) are positive for 1≤L~<L1\leq\tilde{L}<L, showing that the leading coefficient is indeed positive. Since the r.h.s. of Eq. (10) is a second order polynomial with a strictly positive leading term (its graph is an upward-opening parabola), there exists an NN for which this polynomial is positive for any n>Nn>N, i.e., #​params​(n~,L~)>#​params​(n,L)\#\mathrm{params}(\tilde{n},\tilde{L})>\#\mathrm{params}(n,L) for all n>Nn>N. ∎

A.5.1 Critical NN

It is in fact possible to find the critical value NN where the r.h.s. of Eq. (10) vanishes, that is we solve a​n2+b′​n+c=0an^{2}+b^{\prime}n+c=0. The leading coefficient aa is shown in Eq. (11), and other coefficients can be found easily. The coefficients we obtain have common factors and the equation can be factorized as follows: (L−L~)​L~−2​(a~​n2+b~​n+c~)=0(L-\tilde{L})\tilde{L}^{-2}(\tilde{a}n^{2}+\tilde{b}n+\tilde{c})=0, where

a~=2​L​L~−L−L~,b~=−2​a~−L~,c~=a~−L~​(3​L~−1).\tilde{a}=2L\tilde{L}-L-\tilde{L},\quad\tilde{b}=-2\tilde{a}-\tilde{L},\quad\tilde{c}=\tilde{a}-\tilde{L}(3\tilde{L}-1).

It is sufficient to solve a~​n2+b~​n+c~=0\tilde{a}n^{2}+\tilde{b}n+\tilde{c}=0. The largest root is given as a function of L,L~L,\tilde{L}

n0+​(L,L~)=1+L~​(1+12​a~+1)2​a~.n_{0}^{+}(L,\tilde{L})=1+\frac{\tilde{L}(1+\sqrt{12\tilde{a}+1})}{2\tilde{a}}.

where a~\tilde{a}’s dependence in LL and L~\tilde{L} is not noted explicitly to keep the notation compact. The maximal n0+​(L,L~)n_{0}^{+}(L,\tilde{L}) among pairs (L,L~)(L,\tilde{L}) respecting 1≤L~<L1\leq\tilde{L}<L gives NN. We observe that the gradient in LL is always negative

∂n0+∂L=−(6​a~+12​a~+1+1)​L~​(2​L~−1)2​a~2​12​a~+1<0\frac{\partial n_{0}^{+}}{\partial L}=-\frac{\left(6\tilde{a}+\sqrt{12\tilde{a}+1}+1\right)\tilde{L}\left(2\tilde{L}-1\right)}{2\tilde{a}^{2}\sqrt{12\tilde{a}+1}}<0

which is easy to see by noting that a~>0\tilde{a}>0 and L~≥1\tilde{L}\geq 1. This implies that n0+n_{0}^{+} is maximized by setting LL to its smallest possible value, L~+1\tilde{L}+1

n0+​(L~+1,L~)=1+L~​(1+24​L~2−11)4​L~2−2.n_{0}^{+}(\tilde{L}+1,\tilde{L})=1+\frac{\tilde{L}\left(1+\sqrt{24\tilde{L}^{2}-11}\right)}{4\tilde{L}^{2}-2}.

This expression decreases monotonically in L~\tilde{L} for L~≥1\tilde{L}\geq 1. Thus, n0+n_{0}^{+} is again maximized by choosing the appropriate boundary, L~=1\tilde{L}=1. The maximum is n0+​(L=2,L~=1)=(3+13)/2≈3.30n_{0}^{+}(L=2,\tilde{L}=1)=(3+\sqrt{13})/2\approx 3.30, which is rounded up to 44. Therefore, for any depth LL and any hidden size n≥4n\geq 4, there exists a function computable by an RNN with LL layers and nn neurons which cannot be computed by a shallower network without increasing the number of parameters.

A.6 Formalization of "linear BIRNNs compute polynomial transformations"

Proposition.

Let h∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L) be the function computed by a BIRNN. Then, for any TT, the function f:ℝd​T→ℝn​Tf:\mathbb{R}^{dT}\to\mathbb{R}^{nT} mapping (concatenations of) sequences of inputs (𝐱1,⋯,𝐱T)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{T}) to (concatenations of) sequences of hidden states (𝐡1(L),⋯,𝐡T(L))(\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{h}^{(L)}_{T}) is a multivariate polynomial whose order is at most TLT^{L}.

Proof.

First, it is easy to check that ff is a polynomial since the update function of a linear 2RNN is a polynomial map of order 2:

𝐡t(l)=𝓐(l)×1𝐡t−1(l)×2𝐡t(l−1)+𝐕(l)𝐡t−1(l)+𝐔(l)𝐡t(l−1)+𝐛(l).\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(l)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}\times_{2}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}+\mathbf{U}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}.

Thus, each 𝐡t(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} is obtained by composing polynomial maps of the inputs, and ff is itself a polynomial map.

We now proceed to show that the order of the polynomial is at most TLT^{L} by considering the recurrence on LL. For sake of simplicity, we assume that only the second order parameters 𝓐(l)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(l)} of the 2RNN are non-zero, since the polynomial interactions of highest order in 𝐡t(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)} are the second order ones. For L=1L=1, for any tt, we have

𝐡t(1)=𝓣×1𝐡(1)0×2𝐱1×3⋯×t+1𝐱t\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(1)}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{0}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{1}\times_{3}\cdots\times_{t+1}\mathbf{x}_{t}

where the (t+2)(t+2)th order tensor 𝓣∈ℝn×d×⋯×d×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d\times\cdots\times d\times n} is defined by

𝓣i,j1,⋯,jt,k=∑r1=1n∑r2=1n⋯∑r2=1n(𝐡0(1))i𝓐i,j1,r1(1)𝓐r1,j2,r2(1)𝓐r2,j3,r3(1)⋯𝓐rn,jn,k(1)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{i,j_{1},\cdots,j_{t},k}=\sum_{r_{1}=1}^{n}\sum_{r_{2}=1}^{n}\cdots\sum_{r_{2}=1}^{n}(\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{0})_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(1)}_{i,j_{1},r_{1}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(1)}_{r_{1},j_{2},r_{2}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(1)}_{r_{2},j_{3},r_{3}}\cdots\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(1)}_{r_{n},j_{n},k}

for all i,k∈[n],j1,⋯,jn∈[d]i,k\in[n],j_{1},\cdots,j_{n}\in[d]. This shows that, for L=1L=1, ff is a polynomial map of order at most tt. Indeed, recall that

(𝓣×1𝐡0(1)×2𝐱1×3⋯×t+1𝐱t)k=∑i,j1,⋯,jn𝓣i,j1,⋯,jn,k(𝐡0(1))i(𝐱1)j1⋯(𝐱t)jt.(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{0}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{1}\times_{3}\cdots\times_{t+1}\mathbf{x}_{t})_{k}=\sum_{i,j_{1},\cdots,j_{n}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{i,j_{1},\cdots,j_{n},k}(\mathbf{h}^{(1)}_{0})_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{1})_{j_{1}}\cdots(\mathbf{x}_{t})_{j_{t}}.

Now, assuming the result true for all integers strictly less than LL, the output of the (L−1)(L-1)th layer, (𝐡1(L−1),⋯,𝐡T(L−1))(\mathbf{h}^{(L-1)}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{h}^{(L-1)}_{T}), is a polynomial map of the inputs of order at most TL−1T^{L-1}. Using the same argument as for the case L=1L=1, it is straightforward to show that the output of the LLth layer is a polynomial map of (𝐡1(L−1),⋯,𝐡T(L−1))(\mathbf{h}^{(L-1)}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{h}^{(L-1)}_{T}) of order at most TT. Since the composition of two polynomial maps of orders p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}, respectively, is at most p1​p2p_{1}p_{2}, it follows that the output of the LLth layer is a polynomial map of the inputs of order at most TL−1​T=TLT^{L-1}T=T^{L}. ∎

A.7 Proof of Theorem 3

Theorem.

For n>1n>1 and L≥1L\geq 1, ℋBIRNN​(n,L)⊊ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1) for linear BIRNNs.

Proof.
Inclusion:

We begin by showing that for any h∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L), there exists a function h~∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h}, that is ℋBIRNN​(n,L)⊆ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1). Let the function hh be computed by a BIRNN parameterized by {𝓐(l),𝐡0(l)}l=1L\{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(l)},\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L}. We set the first LL layers of the BIRNN computing h~\tilde{h} the same as the one computing hh such that 𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t:

𝓐~=(l)𝓐(l),𝐡~0(l)=𝐡0(l)∀l∈[L].{\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\mkern 5.0mu}\mkern-5.0mu}{}^{(l)}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\quad\forall l\in[L].

Then, for the last layer L+1L+1, it suffices to add residual connections from the LLth layer and set 𝓐~i​j​k=𝟎​ and ​𝐡~0(L+1)=𝟎\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}_{ijk}=\mathbf{0}\text{ and }\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0} to have 𝐡~t(L+1)=𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L+1)}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t which implies h~=h\tilde{h}=h and proves the inclusion ℋBIRNN​(n,L)⊆ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1).

Strict Inclusion:

We show there exists a function h~∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1) that cannot be computed by any function h∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L), that is ℋBIRNN​(n,L)⊅ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L)\not\supset\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1). Let p​o​l​y​(𝐱,k)poly(\mathbf{x},k) denote the set of functions having a polynomial dependency in 𝐱\mathbf{x} of degree up to kk, irrespective of dependencies in other variables. First, we prove by induction that for any h∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L), the second time step output 𝐡2(L)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)} has a polynomial dependency in 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} of degree at most LL, i.e., 𝐡2(L)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,L)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},L) (using a slight abuse of notation):

  • •

    First, observe from Lemma 1 that the hidden states in the first time step are given by

    𝐡1(l)=(∏i=1l(𝓐(i)×1𝐡0(i))⊤)​𝐱1\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{l}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(i)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(i)})^{\top}\right)\mathbf{x}_{1}

    which means that 𝐡1(l)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,1)​∀l\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},1)\;\forall l.

  • •

    In the second time step, Lemma 1 can similarly be used to obtain

    𝐡2(l)=(∏i=1l(𝓐(i)×1𝐡1(i))⊤)​𝐱2.\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(l)}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{l}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(i)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(i)})^{\top}\right)\mathbf{x}_{2}.

    𝐡2(l)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(l)} contains terms with a maximal number of ll factors in {𝐡1(i)}i=1l\{\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{l}, which, given that 𝐡1(l)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,1)\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},1), implies that 𝐡2(l)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,l)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(l)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},l).

Now we prove there exists a function h~∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L+1) such that 𝐡~2(L+1)=diag​(𝐱1)L+1​𝐱2\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{L+1}\mathbf{x}_{2}. We begin with the case n=dn=d and generalize after. Consider the function h~\tilde{h} parameterized by {𝓐~(l)=δi​j​k,𝐡~0(l)=[1,…,1]⊤}l=1L\{\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(l)}=\delta_{ijk},\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=[1,\dots,1]^{\top}\}_{l=1}^{L}. From Lemma 1 and by observing that for any 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝓐~(l)×1𝐲=diag⁡(𝐲)\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(l)}\times_{1}\mathbf{y}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{y}), we obtain:

𝐡~t(l)=(∏i=1ldiag⁡(𝐡~t−1(i)))​𝐱t.\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(l)}=(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1}^{(i)}))\mathbf{x}_{t}.

Given the hidden states initialization, we have diag⁡(𝐡~0(l))=𝐈∀l\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)})=\mathbf{I}\quad\forall l and the hidden states in the first time step become 𝐡~1(l)=𝐱1\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{1}^{(l)}=\mathbf{x}_{1}. Inserting in the expression for 𝐡~2(l)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(l)}, we obtain

𝐡~2(l)=diag​(𝐱1)l​𝐱2.\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(l)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{l}\mathbf{x}_{2}.

This proves that h~\tilde{h} is such that 𝐡~2(L+1)=diag​(𝐱1)L+1​𝐱2\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{L+1}\mathbf{x}_{2}. This function can not be computed by any h∈ℋBIRNN​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BIRNN}}(n,L) as for any such hh, 𝐡2(L)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,L)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},L).

In the case n>dn>d, we set 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=δi​j​k​∀i,j,k∈[1,d]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(1)}_{ijk}=\delta_{ijk}\forall i,j,k\in[1,d] and 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=0∀i,k∈[d+1,n]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}_{ijk}^{(1)}=0\quad\forall i,k\in[d+1,n]. The result will be the same, but with 0 padding on the extra dimensions. In the case n<dn<d, we set 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=δi​j​k​∀j∈[1,n]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(1)}_{ijk}=\delta_{ijk}\forall j\in[1,n] and 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=0∀j∈[n+1,d]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}_{ijk}^{(1)}=0\quad\forall j\in[n+1,d]. The result will be the same, but for the first nn dimensions of the inputs : 𝐡2(L+1)=diag([𝐱1]1:n)L+1[𝐱2]1:n.\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}([\mathbf{x}_{1}]_{1:n})^{L+1}[\mathbf{x}_{2}]_{1:n}.

∎

A.7.1 Theorem 3 for 2RNNs

In the main text, we focused on BIRNNs to isolate the effect of bilinear interactions, but the same proof technique can be used to prove the result for 2RNNs. Here is the adaptation of Theorem 3 for 2RNNs and its proof.

Theorem.

For n>1n>1 and L≥1L\geq 1, ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)⊊ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1) for linear BIRNNs.

Proof.
Inclusion:

We begin by showing that for any h∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L), there exists a function h~∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h}, that is ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)⊆ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1). Let the function hh be computed by a 2RNN parameterized by {𝓐(l),𝐔(l),𝐕(l),𝐛(l),𝐡0(l)}l=1L\{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(l)},\mathbf{U}^{(l)},\mathbf{V}^{(l)},\mathbf{b}^{(l)},\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L}. We set the first LL layers of the 2RNN computing h~\tilde{h} the same as the one computing hh such that 𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t:

𝓐~(l)=𝓐(l),𝐔~(l)=𝐔(l),𝐕~(l)=𝐕(l),𝐛~(l)=𝐛(l),𝐡~0(l)=𝐡0(l)∀l∈[L].\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{U}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{V}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{b}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\quad\forall l\in[L].

Then, the last layer L+1L+1 is set to perform the identity on 𝐡~t(L)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}^{(L)}_{t}:

𝓐~=𝟎,𝐔~(L+1)=𝐈n,𝐕~(L+1)=𝟎,𝐛~(L+1)=𝟎,𝐡~0(L+1)=𝟎\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}=\mathbf{0},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{I}_{n},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0}

We thus have 𝐡~t(L+1)=𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L+1)}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t which implies h~=h\tilde{h}=h and proves the inclusion ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)⊆ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1).

Strict Inclusion:

We show there exists a function h~∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1) that cannot be computed by any function h∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L), that is ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)⊅ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L)\not\supset\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1). Let p​o​l​y​(𝐱,k)poly(\mathbf{x},k) denote the set of functions having a polynomial dependency in 𝐱\mathbf{x} of degree up to kk, irrespective of dependencies in other variables. First, we prove by induction that for any h∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L), the second time step output 𝐡2(L)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)} has a polynomial dependency in 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} of degree at most LL, i.e., 𝐡2(L)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,L)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},L) (using a slight abuse of notation):

  • •

    First, observe from Lemma 1 that the hidden states in the first time step are given by

    𝐡1(l)=(∏i=1l(𝓐(i)×1𝐡0(i))⊤+𝐔(i))​𝐱1+∑j=1l(∏k=j+1l(𝓐(k)×1𝐡0(k))⊤+𝐔(k))​(𝐕(j)​𝐡0(j)+𝐛(j))\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}=(\prod_{i=1}^{l}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(i)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(i)})^{\top}+\mathbf{U}^{(i)})\mathbf{x}_{1}+\sum_{j=1}^{l}(\prod_{k=j+1}^{l}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(k)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(k)})^{\top}+\mathbf{U}^{(k)})(\mathbf{V}^{(j)}\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(j)}+\mathbf{b}^{(j)})

    which means that 𝐡1(l)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,1)​∀l\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},1)\;\forall l.

  • •

    In the second time step, Lemma 1 can similarly be used to obtain

    𝐡2(l)=(∏i=1l(𝓐(i)×1𝐡1(i))⊤+𝐔(i))​𝐱2+∑j=1l(∏k=j+1l(𝓐(k)×1𝐡1(k))⊤+𝐔(l))​(𝐕(j)​𝐡1(j)+𝐛(j)).\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(l)}=(\prod_{i=1}^{l}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(i)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(i)})^{\top}+\mathbf{U}^{(i)})\mathbf{x}_{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{l}(\prod_{k=j+1}^{l}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}^{(k)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(k)})^{\top}+\mathbf{U}^{(l)})(\mathbf{V}^{(j)}\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(j)}+\mathbf{b}^{(j)}).

    𝐡2(l)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(l)} contains terms with a maximal number of ll factors in {𝐡1(i)}i=1l\{\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{l}, which, given that 𝐡1(l)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,1)\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},1), implies that 𝐡2(l)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,l)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(l)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},l).

Now we prove there exists a function h~∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L+1) such that 𝐡~2(L+1)=diag​(𝐱1)L+1​𝐱2\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{L+1}\mathbf{x}_{2}. We begin with the case n=dn=d and generalize after. Consider the function h~\tilde{h} parameterized by {𝓐~(l)=δi​j​k,𝐔~(l)=𝟎,𝐕~(l)=𝟎,𝐛~(l)=𝟎,𝐡~0(l)=[1,…,1]⊤}l=1L\{\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(l)}=\delta_{ijk},\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{0},\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{0},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{0},\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=[1,\dots,1]^{\top}\}_{l=1}^{L}. By keeping only 𝓐~(l)\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(l)} in Lemma 1, we obtain that 𝐡~t(l)=(∏i=1l𝓐~(i)×1𝐡~t−1(i))⊤​𝐱t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(l)}=(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(i)}\times_{1}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1}^{(i)})^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{t}. By observing that for any 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝓐~(l)×1𝐲=diag⁡(𝐲)\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(l)}\times_{1}\mathbf{y}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{y}), this is simplified to

𝐡~t(l)=(∏i=1ldiag⁡(𝐡~t−1(i)))​𝐱t.\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(l)}=(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1}^{(i)}))\mathbf{x}_{t}.

Given the hidden states initialization, we have diag⁡(𝐡~0(l))=𝐈∀l\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)})=\mathbf{I}\quad\forall l and the hidden states in the first time step become 𝐡~1(l)=𝐱1\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{1}^{(l)}=\mathbf{x}_{1}. Inserting in the expression for 𝐡~2(l)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(l)}, we obtain

𝐡~2(l)=diag​(𝐱1)l​𝐱2.\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(l)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{l}\mathbf{x}_{2}.

This proves that h~\tilde{h} is such that 𝐡~2(L+1)=diag​(𝐱1)L+1​𝐱2\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{L+1}\mathbf{x}_{2}. This function can not be computed by any h∈ℋ2​R​N​N​(n,L)h\in\mathcal{H}_{2\mathrm{RNN}}(n,L) as for any such hh, 𝐡2(L)∈p​o​l​y​(𝐱1,L)\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L)}\in poly(\mathbf{x}_{1},L).

In the case n>dn>d, we set 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=δi​j​k​∀i,j,k∈[1,d]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(1)}_{ijk}=\delta_{ijk}\forall i,j,k\in[1,d] and 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=0∀i,k∈[d+1,n]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}_{ijk}^{(1)}=0\quad\forall i,k\in[d+1,n]. The result will be the same, but with 0 padding on the extra dimensions. In the case n<dn<d, we set 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=δi​j​k​∀j∈[1,n]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}^{(1)}_{ijk}=\delta_{ijk}\forall j\in[1,n] and 𝓐~i​j​k(1)=0∀j∈[n+1,d]\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}}_{ijk}^{(1)}=0\quad\forall j\in[n+1,d]. The result will be the same, but for the first nn dimensions of the inputs : 𝐡2(L+1)=diag([𝐱1]1:n)L+1[𝐱2]1:n.\mathbf{h}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}([\mathbf{x}_{1}]_{1:n})^{L+1}[\mathbf{x}_{2}]_{1:n}.

A.8 Proof of Corollary 1

The same proof technique presented in Appendix A.7 for Theorem 3 can be applied to CPBIRNNs. It suffices to replace the parameter weight tensor 𝓐\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}} by the CP decomposition matrices [[𝐀,𝐁,𝐂]][\![\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}]\!] (the formal definition for CP(BI)RNN can be found in Appendix A.1.3).

Corollary.

For n>1n>1, L≥1L\geq 1 and any R~≥R>1\tilde{R}\geq R>1, ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊊ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1,R~)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1,\tilde{R}) for linear CPBIRNNs.

Proof.
Inclusion:

We begin by showing that for any h∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R), there exists a function h~∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1,R)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1,R) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h}, that is ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊆ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1,R)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1,R). Let the function hh be computed by a CPBIRNN parameterized by {𝐀(l),𝐁(l),𝐂(l),𝐡0(l)}l=1L\{\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\mathbf{C}^{(l)},\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L}. We set the first LL layers of the CPBIRNN computing h~\tilde{h} the same as the one computing hh such that 𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t:

𝐀~(l)=𝐀(l),𝐁~(l)=𝐁(l),𝐂~(l)=𝐂(l),𝐡~0(l)=𝐡0(l)∀l∈[L].\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{(l)}=\mathbf{C}^{(l)},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\quad\forall l\in[L].

Then, for the last layer L+1L+1, it suffices to add residual connections from the LLth layer and set 𝐀~(L+1)=𝟎,𝐁~(L+1)=𝟎,𝐂~(L+1)=𝟎​ and ​𝐡~0(L+1)=𝟎\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0},\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0},\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0}\text{ and }\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(L+1)}=\mathbf{0} to have 𝐡~t(L+1)=𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L+1)}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t which implies h~=h\tilde{h}=h and proves the inclusion ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L)⊆ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1).

Strict Inclusion:

We show there exists a function h~∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1,R)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1,R) that cannot be computed by any function h∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R), that is ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊅ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1,R)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\not\supset\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1,R). Now we prove there exists a function h~∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L+1,R)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L+1,R) such that 𝐡~2(L+1)=diag​(𝐱1)L+1​𝐱2\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}^{(L+1)}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{x}_{1})^{L+1}\mathbf{x}_{2}. A.9 Proof of Theorem 4

Theorem.

For n>1n>1, L≥1L\geq 1 and any R≤RmaxR\leq R_{\textrm{max}}, ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊊ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R+1) for linear CPBIRNNs if R<nR<n.

Proof.
Inclusion:

We begin by showing that for any h∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R), there exists a function h~∈ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R+1)\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R+1) such that h=h~h=\tilde{h}, that is ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊆ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R+1). Let the function hh be computed by a CPBIRNN of rank RR parameterized by {𝐀(l),𝐁(l),𝐂(l),𝐡0(l)}l=1L\{\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\mathbf{C}^{(l)},\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^{L}. For a CPBIRNN of rank R+1R+1 computing h~\tilde{h}, we set:

𝐀~i​j(l)=𝐀i​j(l)∀i∈[n],j≥R\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{ij}^{(l)}=\mathbf{A}^{(l)}_{ij}\quad\forall i\in[n],\;j\geq R
𝐁~i​j(l)=𝐁i​j(l)∀i∈[d],j≥R,\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_{ij}^{(l)}=\mathbf{B}_{ij}^{(l)}\quad\forall i\in[d],j\geq R,
𝐂~i​j(l)=𝐂i​j(l)∀i∈[n],j≥R,\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{C}}_{ij}^{(l)}=\mathbf{C}_{ij}^{(l)}\quad\forall i\in[n],j\geq R,
𝐡~0(l)=𝐡0(l),\displaystyle\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)},

and all other dimensions of 𝐀(l),𝐁(l)​ and ​𝐂(l)\mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)}\text{ and }\mathbf{C}^{(l)} to 0, ∀l∈[L]\forall l\in[L]. We thus have 𝐡~t(L)=𝐡t(L)​∀t\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(L)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}\forall t which implies h~=h\tilde{h}=h and proves the inclusion ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊆ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R+1). ∎

Strict Inclusion:

To show strict inclusion, i.e. ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R)⊅ℋCPBIRNN​(n,L,R+1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R)\not\supset\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{CPBIRNN}}(n,L,R+1), first observe that from Lemma 1 and Equation 5,

𝐡1(l)=(∏i=1l([[𝐀,𝐁,𝐂]](i)×1𝐡0(i))⊤)​𝐱1=(∏i=1l[𝐂(i)​diag​(𝐀(i)⊤​𝐡t−1(i))​𝐁(i)⊤])​𝐱1.\mathbf{h}_{1}^{(l)}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{l}([\![\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}]\!]^{(i)}\times_{1}\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(i)})^{\top}\right)\mathbf{x}_{1}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\left[\mathbf{C}^{(i)}\mathrm{diag}({\mathbf{A}^{(i)}}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(i)}){\mathbf{B}^{(i)}}^{\top}\right]\right)\mathbf{x}_{1}.

One can easily check that, independently of ll, for any CPBIRNN of rank RR, the image of the map 𝐱1↦𝐡(L)\mathbf{x}_{1}\mapsto\mathbf{h}^{(L)} has dimension at most RR, i.e. Im⁡(h1​(ℝd))≤R\mathrm{Im}(h_{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))\leq R. To complete the proof for strict inclusion, we only have to show there exists a CPBIRNN of rank R+1R+1 that reaches that limit (Im⁡(h1​(ℝd))=R+1\mathrm{Im}(h_{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))=R+1), since no CPBIRNNs of rank RR could compute this map. It suffices to consider any CPBIRNNs such that diag⁡(𝐀(i)⊤​𝐡0(l)),𝐁(l),𝐂(l)\mathrm{diag}({\mathbf{A}^{(i)}}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{0}^{(l)}),\mathbf{B}^{(l)},\mathbf{C}^{(l)} for l∈[L]l\in[L] are full rank weight matrices.

A.10 Proof of Theorem 5

Before presenting the proof of Theorem 5, we introduce a lemma that will be used in the proof of Theorem 5.

Lemma 4.

Let ff be a function over sequences of dd-dimensional vectors computed by a 2RNN with nn states (n≥dn\geq d) and parameters 𝓐,𝐔=𝟎,𝐕=𝟎,𝐛=𝟎,𝐡0=𝐟0≠𝟎\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}},\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{f}_{0}\neq\mathbf{0} with 𝓐\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}} generic.

Then, the function ff cannot be computed by any RNN with one layer of any width and nonlinear activations applied only in depth.

Proof.

The computation of a 1 layer RNN of hidden size n~\tilde{n} with nonlinear activations ϕ\phi applied only in depth at each time step tt is given by 𝐲t=ϕ⁡(𝐡t)\mathbf{y}_{t}=\phi(\mathbf{h}_{t}) where 𝐡t=𝐔𝐱t+𝐕𝐡t−1+𝐛\mathbf{h}_{t}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\mathbf{V}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}. Here we assume ϕ\phi is a homeomorphism as are most common activation functions (tanh\tanh, sigmoid, ReLU on OPENℝ≥0)\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}). For such a RNN to compute ff, means there exists a linear map ℓ∈ℒn~,n\ell\in\mathcal{L}^{\tilde{n},n} such that 𝐟t=ℓ⁡(𝐲t)\mathbf{f}_{t}=\ell(\mathbf{y}_{t}) for all tt.

Observe that 𝐡t=h⁡(𝐱1,…,𝐱t)\mathbf{h}_{t}=h(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}) with h∈ℒd​t,n~h\in\mathcal{L}^{dt,\tilde{n}} a linear map.

The function ff is a multi-linear mapping of (𝐱1,…,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}). Given its recursive nature, it can be computed as a bilinear map between 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and 𝐟t−1\mathbf{f}_{t-1}, i.e. f:ℝd×ℝn→ℝnf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, with f⁡(𝐱t,𝐟t−1)=(𝓐×2𝐱t)​𝐟t−1f(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{f}_{t-1})=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{t})\mathbf{f}_{t-1}, but computing ft−1f_{t-1} involves a nonlinear operation between (𝐱1,…,𝐱t−1)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t-1}). Indeed, the entries of a matrix obtained by multiplying slices of a generic tensor (i.e. 𝓐\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}) are polynomial functions of the tensor’s entries. Since a nonzero polynomial (over ℝ\mathbb{R}) vanishes only on a set of Lebesgue measure zero (unless it is identically zero) and 𝓐\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}} is generic, all entries of this matrix are nonzero with probability 1. Thus, 𝐟t−1\mathbf{f}_{t-1} is a polynomial of (𝐱1,…,𝐱t−1)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t-1}):

𝐟t−1=(∑i1,…,it−1𝓐:,it−1,:,…𝓐:,i1,:⏟≠0(𝐱t−1)it−1…(𝐱1)i1)𝐟0\mathbf{f}_{t-1}=\left(\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{t-1}}\underbrace{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{:,i_{t-1},:},\dots\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{:,i_{1},:}}_{\neq 0}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1})_{i_{t-1}}\dots(\mathbf{x}_{1})_{i_{1}}\right)\mathbf{f}_{0}

Since ϕ\phi is a homeomorphism, hh must encode (𝐱1,…,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}) in order for 𝐟t=ℓ⁡(𝐲t)\mathbf{f}_{t}=\ell(\mathbf{y}_{t}) for all tt, which can only be the case if n~≥d​t\tilde{n}\geq dt. However, for any (arbitrarily large) n~\tilde{n}, there will always be a tt sufficiently large such that n~<d​t\tilde{n}<dt, and therefore, no such RNN can compute ff.

∎

Theorem.

There exists a function computed by a single-layer 2RNN that cannot be computed by any RNN of arbitrary (finite) depth and width with nonlinear activation applied only in depth.

Proof.

We consider a 1 layer 2RNN of hidden size nn with parameters 𝓐,𝐔=𝟎,𝐕=𝟎,𝐛=𝟎,𝐡0=𝐟0\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}},\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{f}_{0} satisfying the conditions of Lemma 4, computing the function f:(ℝd)n→ℝnf:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} mapping (𝐱1,…,𝐱T)↦(𝐟1,…,𝐟T)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T})\mapsto(\mathbf{f}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{f}_{T}) with the computation at each time step being 𝐟t=(𝓐×2𝐱t)​𝐟t−1\mathbf{f}_{t}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{t})\mathbf{f}_{t-1}. By unrolling the computation, we obtain 𝐟t=(𝓐×2𝐱t)​(𝓐×2𝐱t−1)​…​(𝓐×2𝐱1)​𝐟0\mathbf{f}_{t}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{t})(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\dots(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{1})\mathbf{f}_{0}. The function ff can be viewed as a multi-linear mapping of (𝐱1,…,𝐱T)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T}), and given its recursive nature, it can also be computed as a bilinear map between 𝐱T\mathbf{x}_{T} and 𝐟T−1\mathbf{f}_{T-1}, i.e. f:ℝd×ℝn→ℝnf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, with f⁡(𝐱T,𝐟T−1)=(𝓐×2𝐱T)​𝐟T−1f(\mathbf{x}_{T},\mathbf{f}_{T-1})=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{T})\mathbf{f}_{T-1}. More generally, we can compute 𝐟T=(𝓐×2𝐱T)​…​(𝓐×2𝐱T−i+1)​𝐟T−i\mathbf{f}_{T}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{T})\dots(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{x}_{T-i+1})\mathbf{f}_{T-i}, so f:((ℝd)i×ℝn)→ℝnf:((\mathbb{R}^{d})^{i}\times\mathbb{R}^{n})\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is a multi-linear map of (𝐱T,…,𝐱T−i+1,𝐟T−i)(\mathbf{x}_{T},...,\mathbf{x}_{T-i+1},\mathbf{f}_{T-i}).

Now consider a RNN of hidden size n~\tilde{n}, depth LL and nonlinear activations ϕ(l)\phi^{(l)} applied only in depth that computes at each time step t∈[T]t\in[T] and layer l∈[L]l\in[L]: 𝐲t(l)=ϕ(l)​(𝐡t(l))\mathbf{y}_{t}^{(l)}=\phi^{(l)}(\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}) where 𝐡t(l)=𝐔(l)​𝐲t(l−1)+𝐕(l)​𝐡t−1(l)+𝐛(l)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(l)}=\mathbf{U}^{(l)}\mathbf{y}_{t}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{V}^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{(l)}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}. We assume ϕ(l)\phi^{(l)}’s are homeomorphisms (as are the common activations tanh\tanh, sigmoid and ReLU on ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}).

We will suppose this RNN is capable of computing ff for any sequence length TT and show that it leads to a contradiction.

We write an output 𝐲t(L)\mathbf{y}_{t}^{(L)} that would achieve the computation as 𝐟¯t∈ℝn~\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{\tilde{n}} and suppose that there exists a linear map ℓ∈ℒn~,n\ell\in\mathcal{L}^{\tilde{n},n} to complete the computation 𝐟t=ℓ⁡(𝐟¯t)\mathbf{f}_{t}=\ell(\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{t}) for all t∈[T]t\in[T].

Assume 𝐲t(L)=ϕ(L)​(𝐡t(L))=𝐟¯t​∀t\mathbf{y}_{t}^{(L)}=\phi^{(L)}(\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)})=\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{t}\;\forall t. Then, either (1) 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} encodes the full sequence (𝐱1,…,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}) or (2) 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} encodes the 2RNN state from some previous time step along with all subsequent inputs, i.e., (𝐱t,…,𝐱t−i+1,𝐟t−i)(\mathbf{x}_{t},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t-i+1},\mathbf{f}_{t-i}) for some i∈[t−1]i\in[t-1]. In case (1), since ϕ(l)\phi^{(l)} is a homeomorphism at all layers ll and the dimension of the space of all possible input sequences of length tt, (𝐱1,…,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}), is d​tdt, if 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} encodes (𝐱1,…,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}), it is necessary that 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} lies in a space of dimension at least d​tdt.

However, we can always find tt such that the dimension of 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)}, n~<d​t\tilde{n}<dt, contradicting the dimension condition required for 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} to encode (𝐱1,…,𝐱t)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t}). We thus have to turn to case (2): 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} must encode (𝐱t,…,𝐱t−i+1,𝐟t−i)(\mathbf{x}_{t},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t-i+1},\mathbf{f}_{t-i}).

Recall that 𝐡t(L)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(L)} is a linear map of (𝐲1(L−1),…,𝐲t(L−1))(\mathbf{y}_{1}^{(L-1)},\dots,\mathbf{y}_{t}^{(L-1)}). The information 𝐟t−i\mathbf{f}_{t-i} is thus encoded in (at least) one of the inputs (𝐲t−i(L−1),…,𝐲t(L−1))(\mathbf{y}_{t-i}^{(L-1)},\dots,\mathbf{y}_{t}^{(L-1)}). Without loss of generality, let 𝐲t−j(L−1)\mathbf{y}_{t-j}^{(L-1)} with j≤ij\leq i encode 𝐟t−i\mathbf{f}_{t-i}. We have that 𝐲t−j(L−1)\mathbf{y}_{t-j}^{(L-1)} encodes all the information of (𝐱t−j,…​𝐱t−i,𝐟t−i)(\mathbf{x}_{t-j},\dots\mathbf{x}_{t-i},\mathbf{f}_{t-i}). This implies that one can find ϕ~(L−1)\tilde{\phi}^{(L-1)} such that 𝐲t−j(L−1)=𝐟¯t−j\mathbf{y}_{t-j}^{(L-1)}=\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{t-j}, which in turn implies that a RNN could compute 𝐟¯t\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{t} with L−1L-1 layers. The same argument can then be used to show that if it can be computed with L−1L-1 layers, it can be done with L−2L-2, and so on, until 1 layer.

However, by Lemma 4, the function ff cannot be computed by any 1-layer RNN with activation only in depth: a contradiction. ∎

Appendix B Experimental details

B.1 Copy, copy-sinus and sinus tasks (synthetic experiments)

Given inputs 𝐱t∈ℝ5\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), the copy task presented in Section 4.1 consists of predicting 𝐱t−p\mathbf{x}_{t-p} at each time step, with a lag set to p=8p=8. Similarly, the copy-sinus and sinus tasks consist in predicting sin⁡(ω​𝐱t−p)\sin(\omega\mathbf{x}_{t-p}), with frequency ω=3\omega=3 and lags p=4p=4 and 0, respectively. The training sets contain 10,000 sequences of length 16; the validation and test sets each contain 200 sequences. Models were trained with a batch size of 128, learning rates between 0.001 and 0.002 and early stopping on the validation set with a patience of 400. For the copy task, we studied a linear RNNs, while for the copy-sinus and sinus tasks, we used a RNN with tanh\tanh activation applied only in depth. Weights were initialized from a random uniform distribution, 𝒰⁡[−1n,1n]\mathcal{U}[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}]. Figures 6 and 7 show the average values over 3–5 random seeds, with the standard deviation indicated by the shaded area. All experiments were run using one GPU (RTX8000, L40S or V100) with 32GB of memory. Generating one point took less than 30 minutes for the shortest experiments (copy) and less than 1.5 hours for the longest (copy-sinus).

B.2 Parity (synthetic experiments)

To produce inputs for the parity task, we take the signs of 𝐱t∈ℝ5\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), resulting in vectors of filled with −1-1s and 1s. The training set contains 10,000 sequences of length 20; the validation and test sets each contain 2000 sequences. The targets consist in element-wise products of the input sequences: 𝐲t=𝐱1​…​𝐱t\mathbf{y}_{t}=\mathbf{x}_{1}...\mathbf{x}_{t}. Models were trained with a batch size of 128, a learning rate 0.001 (0.0005 for few runs) and early stopping with a patience of 400 on the validation set. Figure 8 displays the mean values computed over 3–5 random seeds, with the shaded region representing the standard deviation. We studied RNNs with tanh\tanh activation applied either in depth or in recurrence, with weights were initialized from a uniform distribution, 𝒰⁡[−1n,1n]\mathcal{U}[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}]. Experiments were run on a single GPU (RTX8000, L40S or V100) with 32GB of memory, and it took between 10 minutes and 2 hours for each point.

B.3 Language modeling experiments - Tiny Shakespeare

Language modeling experiments were conducted on the Tiny Shakespeare dataset Karpathy [2015] at the character level, using an embedding size of 107. The dataset was split into training, validation and test sets with a ratio of 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1, respectively. Models were trained on sequences of length 64, with early stopping based on validation performance and a patience of 200 epochs. If the training loss plateaued before showing any learning (i.e., decreasing a reasonable amount), optimization was restarted. In Figure 9, we present the average values over 3–5 random seeds, with the standard deviation shown as a shaded area. All experiments were run on a single GPU (RTX8000, L40S or V100) with 32GB of memory, and training times ranged from 40 minutes to 6 hours.

RNNs and CPRNNs were initialized with weights drawn from a uniform distribution, 𝒰⁡[−1n,1n]\mathcal{U}[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}], and had tanh\tanh activation in the recurrent connections. For RNNs, a batch size of 128 and a learning rate of 0.001 were set across all depths and hidden sizes. For CPRNNs, two optimization regimes were adopted to ensure stability: one with a higher learning rate (0.0005 - 0.001) and a batch size of 128, and another with a lower learning (0.0001) and batch size of 32. The former was used for all hidden sizes at L=1L=1, as well as for n=[64,128,256]n=[64,128,256] at L=2L=2 and L=4L=4. The latter was required for the larger models with n=[512,1024]n=[512,1024] at L=2L=2 and L=4L=4. Similarly, the rank was set to twice the hidden size for all configurations at L=1L=1, except for n=1024n=1024, and for n=[64,128]n=[64,128] at L=2L=2 and L=4L=4. In all other cases, the rank was set equal to the hidden size. S4 models used the diagonal-plus-low-rank kernel Gu et al. [2022], GeLU activation, input normalization, and a dropout rate of 0.1. These models were trained with a learning rate of 0.0001 and a batch size of 32.

B.4 Long Range Arena Benchmark on S4

All experiments on the Long Range Arena benchmark Tay et al. [2021] were conducted using S4 models based on the official implementation from the original S4 paper Gu et al. [2021]. We used an RTX8000 GPU with 48GB of memory. Each run for the shortest experiment (ListOps) took between 5 and 10 hours, while for Retrieval and Images it ranged between 15 to 35 hours. The longest, Pathfinder, required between 30 and 60 hours.

All parameters, except for the depth LL and number of features HH, were kept the same as the original settings for each tasks. The depth used in the original paper was L=6L=6, for our purposes, we varied the depth from 2 to 8 and adjusted the number of features HH to maintain a constant parameter count (see Table 2).
